stops.name: Zhaoqing, granted a plot by the pagoda
stops.campa: The governor of Zhaoqing, Wang Pan, who has heard of the foreigners' learning, grants Ruggieri and Ricci land beside the Chongxi Pagoda to build a residence, the first permanent Catholic house allowed inside China proper in living memory. They raise it in the style of a Buddhist monastery and call it Xianhua Si, the Temple of the Flower of the Immortals; Ricci wears the shaved head and grey robe of a Buddhist monk, believing, as the mission still believes at this hour, that the bonze's dress is the nearest thing China offers to a holy man's habit.

stops.name: Zhaoqing, the map of ten thousand countries
stops.campa: At the request of Governor Wang Pan, who wants a resource for scholars and travelers, Ricci draws the first map in Chinese to show the whole round earth after the European fashion, the Yudi Shanhai Quantu: continents, seas and the great southern unknown all lettered in careful characters. It startles Zhaoqing's literati, who have never seen China rendered as one country among many rather than as the whole civilized world with barbarian fringes at its edge. Ricci will spend the rest of his life refining this single sheet, and its final Peking version will still be read three centuries on.

stops.name: Zhaoqing, the clock, the prism, and the mandarins
stops.campa: Ricci wins the province's curiosity with instruments no one south of Macau has seen: a self-striking clock that tells the hour without a hand to ring it, a prism that unbraids the sun into every color at once, sundials, spheres, a world atlas. Mandarins and their sons crowd the house to see these things and stay to hear the Italian father speak, in careful literary Chinese, of one Lord who made the heavens the instruments only imitate. The gifts are a door; the doctrine that follows through it is the whole of the mission's design.

stops.name: Zhaoqing, cast out by the new viceroy
stops.campa: Six years of patient building end when a new viceroy, hostile to the foreigners and covetous of their now-famous house, orders the Jesuits from Zhaoqing entirely, offering only enough silver to cover the journey. Ricci and his companions are driven out with what they can carry, leaving the fine house, the church, and the converts behind them. It is the first of the mission's several expulsions, and Ricci records it without despair: the door south has shut, but he reads it, as he reads every reversal in China, as a push further into the empire rather than out of it.

stops.name: Shaozhou, a house on the Bei River
stops.campa: Expelled south, Ricci obtains leave to settle instead at Shaozhou, further up the Bei River and further from the coastal officials who distrust the trade with Macau. He builds again from nothing, a house, a small church, a school where he now teaches mathematics openly to whichever scholars will come, using it, as at Zhaoqing, as the bait that draws literate China toward the doctrine underneath. The province is poorer and rougher than Guangdong, but further inland, which is exactly what the long strategy toward Peking requires.

stops.name: Shaozhou, the night of the robbers
stops.campa: One night thieves break into the mission house, believing the foreigners keep silver made by their alchemy; in the struggle Ricci is struck and badly hurt, his skull and hand injured, and for a time his life is feared for. He counts the attack among the trials God permits to test the mission rather than to end it, and recovers slowly through the summer, marked afterward, his companions say, by a scar and by an even greater equanimity toward danger. The same rumor of foreign gold that draws Qu Taisu to his door had very nearly killed him first.

stops.name: Shaozhou, Qu Taisu and the rudiments of Euclid
stops.campa: Qu Taisu, a scholar's son drawn first by rumor of the foreigners' alchemy, becomes instead Ricci's student in mathematics and his sponsor among the Confucian literati of Guangdong. Ricci teaches him the elements of Euclid's geometry, translated on the spot into literary Chinese, the first time the West's deductive method is laid before a Chinese mind in its own tongue. In exchange Qu opens the circles of the mandarins to him and, watching the Italian sweat under his monk's robe at a scholars' banquet, gives him the one piece of advice that will remake the whole mission's face.

stops.name: Shaozhou, the robe of the literati
stops.campa: Ricci and his companion Lazzaro Cattaneo lay aside the shaved head and grey habit of the Buddhist bonze and put on the silk gown, the black gauze cap, and the long hair and beard of a Confucian scholar, taking for himself the courtesy name Xitai, Master from the West. It is a complete change of face: the bonze is a figure of low repute among the mandarins, the scholar a figure of the highest honor. The doctrine has not changed a word, but the door it must pass through has been recut entirely to Chinese specification.

stops.name: North from Shaozhou, over the Meiling Pass
stops.campa: With a mandarin patron bound for the war ministry at Nanjing, Ricci finally leaves the south, crossing the Meiling Pass into the Gan river valley on the road every literatus takes toward the Yangtze and the capital. Twelve years after Zhaoqing he is at last moving toward the empire's center rather than its edge, carrying the accumulated instruments, the finished maps, and the reputation of a Western sage that Qu Taisu and the mandarins of Guangdong have spent a decade building for him. Peking is still six years and two rebuffs away, though he does not yet know the count.

stops.name: Nanjing, turned back at the southern capital
stops.campa: Ricci's patron dies en route, and he arrives at Nanjing, the Ming's southern capital, alone and without protection, at the worst possible hour: the court is at war with Japan over Korea and deeply suspicious of any foreigner near a capital, however secondary. Officials who a year before might have welcomed a curiosity now see a possible spy; he is warned off and told to leave the city within days. It is the first of three checks the road to Peking will deal him, and he turns west instead, toward Nanchang and the province of Jiangxi.

stops.name: Nanchang, a house among the princes of the blood
stops.campa: In Nanchang, capital of Jiangxi and seat of several collateral branches of the Ming imperial house, Ricci finds a warmer welcome than Nanjing gave him: the governor and the resident princes, remote from Peking's wartime suspicion and hungry for novelty, take him up as a curiosity of the first order, a Confucian-dressed Westerner who speaks their classics and draws the whole world on a single sheet of paper. Within months he has the freedom of the city's scholarly society and the beginnings of the reputation, the Sage of the Great West, that will carry him the rest of the way north.

stops.name: Nanchang, a treatise on friendship for the Prince of Jian'an
stops.campa: At a banquet given by Zhu Duojie, Prince of the Jian'an commandery and a distant cousin of the Wanli Emperor, Ricci is asked what the men of the Great West think of friendship. He answers with a small book, a hundred maxims gathered and paraphrased from Aristotle, Cicero, Seneca and the Christian fathers and rendered into elegant literary Chinese, which he presents to the prince as a gift. It circulates far beyond the palace, copied and admired by scholars who have never met a Westerner, the first work of a European's authorship to enter general Chinese literary circulation.
stops.quote: My friend is not an other, but half of myself, and thus a second me — I must therefore regard my friend as myself.
stops.quote_source: Ricci, Jiaoyou Lun (On Friendship, 1595), maxim 1, tr. Timothy Billings, On Friendship: One Hundred Maxims for a Chinese Prince
